title: Raga Sarang
hook: a raga for the hot middle of the day, and a Guru who calls himself a servant

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ramanand's hymn in Basant: he set out for the temple with sandalwood and was shown God in his own heart. Your line was spring at home. What in your own place was worth staying for? Day one thousand one hundred sixteen.

Noon on a hot street. The shadow of a lamppost has shrunk to a dark puddle at its foot. Shopkeepers pull down awnings. Phones buzz, inboxes fill, and the day is at its loudest and its busiest, with half of it gone and half still to do. Morning ragas get the dawn and evening ragas get the dusk, but the Guru Granth Sahib also has a raga that tradition gives to this hour, the hot, bright middle. It's called Sarang. Today: Raga Sarang, and what its first hymn does with the busiest part of the day.
screen: `NOON ON A HOT STREET.` → `THE DAY AT ITS LOUDEST.` → `RAGA SARANG.`

segments.voice: Where we are: Sarang follows Basant in the Granth's order, so the book moves from spring to the heat of the day. Tradition sings Sarang in the midday hours, and later in the section there's also a Var, a ballad of stanzas with saloks between them, by Guru Ram Das. The section opens with a hymn of Guru Nanak, and its first line is a surprise from a Guru. In paraphrase: I am the servant girl of my own Master. I have taken hold of the feet of God, the life of the world, and my ego has been settled and put to rest. The Guru speaks of himself as a servant, and a humble one. In the Granth the Gurus sometimes speak in the voice of a bride or a servant before God, and here the picture is of someone who has stopped running the house and is simply holding on to the Master. Now set that at noon. Midday is when the self is busiest: deciding, answering, pushing the list along. It's the hour when it's easiest to feel like the one in charge of everything. The opening of Sarang puts a different picture at the center of that hour. Not someone on top of the day, but someone holding on to the feet of the One who gives the world its life, with the ego quiet. That doesn't mean stopping work. In the hymn's picture, the work goes on, but the house has a Master, and it isn't the servant. A shadow at noon is small, because the sun is right overhead. The hymn's ego is small for the same reason. Today's line: midday.
screen: `AFTER BASANT: THE HEAT OF THE DAY.` · `I AM THE SERVANT OF MY OWN MASTER.` · `HOLDING THE FEET, EGO AT REST.` · `A SMALL SHADOW AT NOON.` · then, large: `MIDDAY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: listen at midday. If it's around noon now, play a shabad sung in Raga Sarang, or sit in the quiet. If it isn't, set a reminder for the middle of today and come back to this then. Wherever you are when you do it, stop what you're running. Put your hands down, palms open, as if you've set down the keys to the whole operation. Breathe slowly. Notice how much of you was busy being in charge, and let some of it rest. If you pray, you can hold Guru Nanak's picture of holding the Master's feet. If you don't, simply let the open hands do the work. The bell holds the time.
Raga Sarang. The raga that follows Basant, sung by tradition in the midday hours, opening with Guru Nanak's line that he is the servant of his own Master, with his ego put to rest. Today's word.
Your line: midday. At the busiest point of today, take ten seconds with open hands before the next task, and let the day rest on more than you alone. Day one thousand one hundred sixteen.

howItsDone: In kirtan, shabads from the Sarang section of the Guru Granth Sahib are sung in Raga Sarang, which tradition associates with the midday hours, and the Var of Sarang is sung or read in the sangat.
